summary: Discusses issues in deploying IPv6 in mobile networks, where smartphones and other mobile devices accelerate IPv4 address exhaustion. It is a reference for service providers and network designers and replaced RFC 6312.

eli5.summary: Phones are using up the old internet addresses fast, so the new kind is needed. This guide helps phone companies plan the move.

questions: where to place nat in a mobile network
subtitle: What phone operators have to think about when they move their networks from IPv4 to IPv6.

tldr.problem: Mobile Internet growth is using up IPv4 addresses, and mobile networks have quirks (gateways, roaming, billing) that make IPv6 deployment harder than in fixed networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through address exhaustion, where to put NAT (centralized, distributed or hybrid), IPv6-only deployment with roaming and VoLTE, and fixed-mobile convergence, using existing solutions. It proposes no new protocols.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational reference for operators and network designers. It obsoletes RFC 6312, which carried the wrong RFC number in its header; the specification is otherwise unchanged.

today: RFC 6342 is an Informational RFC and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It replaced RFC 6312, which had the wrong RFC number in its header.

sections.title: Why Mobile Networks Need Their Own Advice
sections.content:
RFC 6342 says that the dramatic growth of the Mobile Internet is accelerating the exhaustion of available IPv4 addresses, and that IPv6 is necessary for the Internet's continued operation and growth. IPv6 brings many benefits, but mobile networks add challenges of their own.

The document describes those challenges and the applicability of existing IPv6 deployment solutions. It does not propose any new protocols or new protocol work. It mostly assumes the 3GPP 3G and 4G architectures, though it says the considerations are general enough for other mobile architectures.

It is a revised copy of RFC 6312. Because of a publishing error, RFC 6312 had the wrong RFC number in its header, so this document corrects that with a new number. The specification is otherwise unchanged.
sections.eli5: Phone companies are running out of the old kind of address. This paper does not invent anything new. It explains how to use the tools that already exist.

sections.title: The Reference Mobile Network
sections.content:
The RFC defines a reference architecture. A Mobile Node (MN) reaches the network through its Home Network or, when roaming, a Visited Network. In 3GPP, the MN connects through an Access Point Name (APN), which maps to a mobile gateway and says which services and which kind of IP connectivity (IPv4, IPv6 or IPv4v6) are allowed.

The end-to-end link to the gateway is an EPS bearer in LTE or a PDP context in 3G UMTS. Along the way are several nodes:

  • Base Station (BS): gives the MN wireless connectivity.
  • Access Network Gateway (ANG): forwards IP packets but is typically not the MN's default router and does not allocate addresses.
  • Mobile Network Gateway (MNG): the MN's default router. It manages IP addresses and does subscriber management such as QoS, policy, billing and accounting.
  • Border Router (BR): borders the Internet and does no subscriber management.
  • AAA and PCRF: authentication, authorization and accounting, and policy and charging rules applied at the MNG.
sections.eli5: A phone talks to a tower, which passes its messages along a chain of helpers. One helper in the middle hands out addresses and keeps the bills, and another sits at the edge facing the Internet.

sections.title: IPv4 Exhaustion and Dual-Stack
sections.content:
Providers have two parallel options: delay IPv4 exhaustion by conserving addresses, and introduce IPv6. Conserving means private IPv4 addresses for users behind a provider-side NAT, or port-range extensions that need tunneling and extra signaling. The RFC focuses on translation, namely NAT44 (public to private IPv4) and NAT64 (IPv6 to IPv4), because 3GPP already has tunneling in GTP and allows dual-stack and IPv6-only deployments.

In LTE an always-on PDN connection is needed to reach a user, which is required to support Voice over IP. If that connection used IPv4, every attached MN would consume a private IPv4 address. One answer is to make the always-on PDN IPv6 and bring up the IPv4 PDN only when needed. 3GPP also specifies deferred IPv4 allocation on a dual-stack IPv4v6 PDN, but this needs DHCP-style support and triggers that the RFC says did not exist in mobile phones at the time.

In pre-Release-8 3G UMTS, dual-stack PDP connections are not supported, so two separate PDP connections are needed for IPv4 and IPv6. The RFC concludes that the IETF dual-stack model applies readily, with a single IPv4v6 PDN from Release-8 onwards and separate PDP contexts before that, and that operators can make IPv6 the default for always-on connections.
sections.eli5: Every phone that stays connected would use up one of the scarce old addresses. So companies can give phones the new kind by default and hand out an old one only when it is really needed.

sections.title: Where to Put the NAT
sections.content:
The private IPv4 space is not abundant for a large mobile network: the NET10 block from RFC 1918 has about 16.7 million addresses, and a large operator can have more subscribers than that attached at once. NAT also matters for billing and policy, because a NAT creates a binding between two addresses. The PCRF may need to inspect that binding to tell individual MNs apart, and there may be legal requirements to store the records.

The RFC compares three placements:

  • Centralized: one NAT and address pool shared by several MNGs, usually at the BR. It reuses private space and suits legacy deployments, but needs overlapping addresses handled with tunnels (GRE, MPLS VPN or IP-in-IP), extra protocols to correlate NAT state with subscriber sessions, and the NAT is a single point of failure.
  • Distributed: each MNG manages its own NET10 block and does the NAT. Unique addresses in the core, easy correlation with AAA and PCRF, but no central management of NAT.
  • Hybrid: a dedicated NAT device, behaving like either model depending on whether its pool is unique or overlapping, and it must report bindings to an external entity such as AAA or PCRF.

The RFC says providers wanting easy integration with subscriber management may find the distributed model compelling, while those wanting common NAT management may prefer the centralized one.
sections.eli5: Imagine one shared mailroom for the whole company or a small mailroom on every floor. The shared one is easier to manage, but the floor ones keep track of who sent what much more easily.

sections.title: IPv6-Only Deployment and Roaming
sections.content:
The RFC treats NAT as an interim solution. It describes three dimensions of an IPv6-only move: the network, the mobile nodes and the applications. The classic dual-stack path is the least disruptive but implies large-scale NAT and separate PDP contexts in 3G. Another path has an IPv6-only network and MN with mostly IPv4 applications, which ironically needs IPv6-to-IPv4 translation. That needs no overlap handling, since IPv6 addresses are unique, but it does need DNS64 (RFC 6147) so that synthesized AAAA records point at the translator. RFC 6146 and RFC 6145 apply when translators are used.

Applications are a long-tail problem, including IPv4 literals in protocols such as XMPP or in HTML and XML content. VoLTE adds its own issues, since voice signaling is generally free while the call itself is charged by duration, and this model is expected to work during roaming.

Roaming is the biggest mobile-specific complication. A provider cannot control its roaming partners' networks. An IPv6-only LTE operator must still offer IPv4 for its outbound roamers who visit networks without IPv6, and for inbound roamers whose devices lack IPv6. Even so, introducing IPv6-only for newer MNs can significantly reduce demand for private IPv4 addresses.
sections.eli5: Switching everything to the new addresses at once would leave some visitors and old phones stranded. So companies switch the new phones first and keep a back door for the rest.

sections.title: Fixed-Mobile Convergence and Conclusions
sections.content:
Many providers run both fixed and mobile networks, but the two differ. Roaming is not a fixed-network concern, voice is required of an all-IP mobile provider but not a fixed one, and not every mobile link can carry both IPv4 and IPv6. Solutions differ too. Tunneling private IPv4 inside IPv6 works where the endpoint is a cable or DSL modem, not where the endpoint is the MN itself. 6rd (RFC 5969) suits fixed networks that cannot offer native IPv6, whereas mobile networks can reuse their existing tunneling.

The RFC concludes that the provider's core network is the most likely place for convergence, with similar gains at the service and application layers. It also notes that a Femto Base Station behind a private IPv4 NAT is exposed to NAT policy such as periodic purging of state.

The Security Considerations section says only that the document does not introduce any new security vulnerabilities.
sections.eli5: Home internet and phone internet are cousins, not twins. They can share the big pipes in the middle, but each needs its own kind of plug at the end.
